section.title: The Sun Stands Still
section.sectionRationale: Israel's treaty with Gibeon draws it into war. Five Amorite kings attack Gibeon, and Israel marches all night to defend its new ally. God routs the enemy, hurls hailstones from heaven, and answers Joshua's astonishing prayer by making the sun stand still. The five kings are captured and executed, and the whole southern region falls in a single campaign. It is one movement, the southern conquest crowned by the day the sun stood still, in which the LORD Himself fights for Israel.
section.thesis: The conquest of the south is unmistakably the LORD's doing: He throws the enemy into panic, kills more by hailstones than by swords, halts sun and moon at the prayer of a man, and gives all the land in one campaign, so that the glory belongs to the God who fights for His people, not to Israel's armies.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the coalition attacks Gibeon and Israel marches to help, verses 1 to 9; the LORD routs the enemy with hail, verses 10 to 11; the sun stands still at Joshua's prayer, verses 12 to 15; the five kings captured and executed, verses 16 to 27; and the southern cities conquered in one campaign, verses 28 to 43.

units.label: The coalition attacks Gibeon and Israel marches to help
units.note: do not be afraid; I have delivered them into your hand

verses.text: Now Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem heard that Joshua had captured Ai and devoted it to destruction, doing to Ai and its king as he had done to Jericho and its king, and that the people of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were living near them.
So Adoni-zedek and his people were greatly alarmed, because Gibeon was a great city, like one of the royal cities; it was larger than Ai, and all its men were mighty.
Therefore Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent word to Hoham king of Hebron, Piram king of Jarmuth, Japhia king of Lachish, and Debir king of Eglon, saying,
“Come up and help me. We will attack Gibeon, because they have made peace with Joshua and the Israelites.”
So the five kings of the Amorites, the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon, joined forces and advanced with all their armies. They camped before Gibeon and made war against it.

Then the men of Gibeon sent word to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal: “Do not abandon your servants. Come quickly and save us! Help us, because all the kings of the Amorites from the hill country have joined forces against us.”
So Joshua and his whole army, including all the mighty men of valor, came from Gilgal.
The LORD said to Joshua, “Do not be afraid of them, for I have delivered them into your hand. Not one of them shall stand against you.”
After marching all night from Gilgal, Joshua caught them by surprise.

units.label: The LORD routs the enemy with hail
units.note: more were killed by the hailstones than by the sword

verses.text: And the LORD threw them into {{hamam|confusion}} before Israel, who defeated them in a great slaughter at Gibeon, pursued them along the ascent to Beth-horon, and struck them down as far as Azekah and Makkedah.

As they fled before Israel along the descent from Beth-horon to Azekah, the LORD cast down on them large hailstones from the sky, and more of them were killed by the hailstones than by the swords of the Israelites.

units.label: The sun stands still at Joshua's prayer
units.note: there has been no day like it, for the LORD fought for Israel

verses.text: On the day that the LORD gave the Amorites over to the Israelites, Joshua spoke to the LORD in the presence of Israel: “O sun, stand still over Gibeon, O moon, over the Valley of Aijalon.”

So the sun {{damam|stood still}} and the moon stopped until the nation took vengeance upon its enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar? “So the sun stopped in the middle of the sky and delayed going down about a full day.”
There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD listened to the voice of a man, because the LORD fought for Israel.
Then Joshua returned with all Israel to the camp at Gilgal.

units.label: The five kings captured and executed
units.note: put your feet on the necks of these kings

verses.text: Now the five kings had fled and hidden in the cave at Makkedah.
And Joshua was informed: “The five kings have been found; they are hiding in the cave at Makkedah.”
So Joshua said, “Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave, and post men there to guard them.
But you, do not stop there. Pursue your enemies and attack them from behind. Do not let them reach their cities, for the LORD your God has delivered them into your hand.”
So Joshua and the Israelites continued to inflict a terrible slaughter until they had finished them off, and the remaining survivors retreated to the fortified cities.
The whole army returned safely to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah, and no one dared to utter a word against the Israelites.
Then Joshua said, “Open the mouth of the cave and bring those five kings out to me.”
So they brought the five kings out of the cave, the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon.

When they had brought the kings to Joshua, he summoned all the men of Israel and said to the army commanders who had accompanied him, “Come here and put your feet on the necks of these kings.” So the commanders came forward and put their feet on their necks.
“Do not be afraid or discouraged,” Joshua said. “Be strong and courageous, for the LORD will do this to all the enemies you fight.”
After this, Joshua struck down and killed the kings, and he hung their bodies on five trees and left them there until evening.

At sunset Joshua ordered that they be taken down from the trees and thrown into the cave in which they had hidden. Then large stones were placed against the mouth of the cave, and the stones are there to this day.

units.label: The southern cities conquered in one campaign

verses.text: On that day Joshua captured Makkedah and put it to the sword, along with its king. He devoted to destruction everyone in the city, leaving no survivors. So he did to the king of Makkedah as he had done to the king of Jericho.
Then Joshua and all Israel with him moved on from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against Libnah.

And the LORD also delivered that city and its king into the hand of Israel, and Joshua put all the people to the sword, leaving no survivors. And he did to the king of Libnah as he had done to the king of Jericho.
And Joshua and all Israel with him moved on from Libnah to Lachish. They laid siege to it and fought against it.
And the LORD delivered Lachish into the hand of Israel, and Joshua captured it on the second day. He put all the people to the sword, just as he had done to Libnah.
At that time Horam king of Gezer went to help Lachish, but Joshua struck him down along with his people, leaving no survivors.
So Joshua moved on from Lachish to Eglon, and all Israel with him. They laid siege to it and fought against it.
That day they captured Eglon and put it to the sword, and Joshua devoted to destruction everyone in the city, just as he had done to Lachish.
Then Joshua and all Israel with him went up from Eglon to Hebron and fought against it.
They captured it and put to the sword its king, all its villages, and all the people. Joshua left no survivors, just as he had done at Eglon; he devoted to destruction Hebron and everyone in it.
Finally Joshua and all Israel with him turned toward Debir and fought against it.

And they captured Debir, its king, and all its villages. They put them to the sword and devoted to destruction everyone in the city, leaving no survivors. Joshua did to Debir and its king as he had done to Hebron and as he had done to Libnah and its king.

So Joshua conquered the whole region, the hill country, the Negev, the foothills, and the slopes, together with all their kings, leaving no survivors. He {{cherem|devoted to destruction}} everything that breathed, just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded.
Joshua conquered the area from Kadesh-barnea to Gaza, and the whole region of Goshen as far as Gibeon.
And because the LORD, the God of Israel, {{lacham|fought}} for Israel, Joshua captured all these kings and their land in one campaign.
Then Joshua returned with all Israel to the camp at Gilgal.

hamam.gloss: To throw into confusion, panic, or rout. The LORD Himself hamam the Amorite armies, the same word used of His routing Egypt at the sea and Sisera's host. The decisive blow is not Israel's night march but God sowing panic among the enemy; the victory is His before a sword falls, and Israel merely pursues a foe God has already broken.

damam.gloss: To be still, to stand silent or motionless, to cease. At Joshua's word the sun damam, stood still, and the moon stopped, so that the day of battle was extended. However one understands the mechanics, the text presents it as an unrepeatable wonder in answer to prayer, evidence that the God who fights for Israel commands even the sun and moon, the very lights the Canaanites worshiped.

cherem.gloss: That which is devoted irrevocably to the LORD, here by destruction. City after city of the south is placed under the cherem as God's judgment on Canaan's entrenched wickedness, carried out just as the LORD commanded. The repeated ban marks the conquest as an act of divine justice under God's authority, not human aggression or greed.

lacham.gloss: To fight, do battle, wage war. The chapter's refrain is that the LORD lacham for Israel; He is the true warrior, and Joshua's armies win because God fights on their behalf. This is the theological heart of the whole conquest: the land is taken not by Israel's might but by the LORD who fights for His people and gives them the victory.

basic.context: Because Gibeon made peace with Israel, five Amorite kings unite to punish it, and Gibeon calls Israel for help. Joshua marches his army all night and takes the enemy by surprise. Then God takes over the battle: He throws the enemy into panic, kills more of them with giant hailstones than Israel kills with the sword, and, in answer to Joshua's bold prayer, makes the sun stand still so the day of victory is extended. The narrator says there was never a day like it, because the LORD fought for Israel. The five kings are captured, executed, and Joshua tells his commanders to put their feet on their necks as a sign of total victory. Then, city by city, the whole south falls in a single campaign. The question underneath is: who really wins Israel's battles?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, and its refrain interprets it: the LORD fought for Israel. The famous sun standing still is reported as a genuine, unrepeatable wonder, and Christians debate its mechanics without doubting God's power over creation. The chapter also intensifies the herem, the devoting of cities to destruction, which must be read honestly as God's judgment on Canaan. We do not draw rules for warfare from it; we learn that the victory belongs to God.
basic.originalLanguages: The LORD hamam, throws the enemy into panic; the sun damam, stands still, at Joshua's prayer; city after city is placed under the cherem, devoted to destruction; and the refrain is that the LORD lacham, fought, for Israel.
basic.typology: God fighting for His people and subduing kings points to Christ, who fights the true battle and puts all His enemies under His feet. The feet on the necks of the kings foreshadows the final subjection of every enemy beneath the feet of Christ and His people. The victory won not by human strength pictures the salvation accomplished by God alone.
basic.christ: The LORD who fights for Israel and crushes the kings foreshadows Christ, who conquers sin, death, and the powers, and under whose feet every enemy will be placed, 1 Corinthians 15:25. Joshua's word to fearful commanders, do not be afraid, be strong, for the LORD will do this to all your enemies, echoes forward to the assurance believers have that Christ has overcome the world.
basic.god: God is the divine warrior who fights for His people, commanding hail from heaven and even halting the sun. He is sovereign over creation, listening to a man's prayer and bending the heavens. And He is the righteous Judge, bringing His long-warned judgment on Canaan through Israel. The victory and the glory are entirely His.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 14 shows the LORD fighting for Israel at the sea while they are still. Psalm 18 pictures God routing enemies with hail and thunder. 1 Corinthians 15 declares Christ reigning until all enemies are under His feet. And Romans 16 promises God will soon crush Satan under His people's feet.
basic.oneStory: The southern conquest is won not by Israel's armies but by the LORD, who panics the enemy, rains hail, halts the sun, and gives the whole land in one campaign. It is a vivid display of God as the warrior who fights for His people, pointing forward to Christ, who wins the decisive victory and puts every enemy under His feet.

context.literary:
The chapter is built around a single sentence that appears twice, in verse 14 and again in verse 42, there has been no day like it and the LORD fought for Israel, and everything between those two markers is arranged to prove the claim rather than merely state it. The opening section, verses 1 to 9, is heavy with speech, Adoni-zedek's summons to the other kings, Gibeon's plea, and finally the LORD's own word to Joshua, do not be afraid, so that before a single blow is struck the reader already knows how the battle will end; suspense is deliberately removed so that attention falls entirely on why Israel wins rather than whether it will.

The battle report itself, verses 10 to 15, is compressed and almost breathless, three separate divine interventions crowded into six verses, panic sown among the enemy, hailstones killing more than swords, and the sun and moon held motionless, each one escalating past the last so that a reader who might explain away one miracle has two others to account for. The poetic fragment quoted from the Book of Jashar in verse 13 marks the center of the whole chapter as a moment of celebrated wonder, framed by the narrator's own comment that there had been no day like it before or since. What follows, the capture of the cave, verses 16 to 27, and the formulaic list of southern cities, verses 28 to 43, deliberately flattens back into repetitive, almost liturgical prose, city after city falling with the identical phrase and the LORD delivered, a stylistic choice that keeps crediting God even after the miraculous has given way to ordinary siege warfare, so that the chapter's theology governs its plainest verses just as much as its most spectacular ones.
context.historical:
Adoni-zedek, whose name means lord of righteousness or my lord is Zedek, ruled Jerusalem, a name that itself recalls an earlier king of that city, Melchizedek, king of righteousness, in Genesis 14:18, suggesting royal titles at Jerusalem may have run in this pattern for generations before David ever took the city. He assembles four other kings from cities across the southern hill country and lowlands, forming a coalition alarmed enough by Gibeon's defection to risk direct confrontation with Israel rather than wait to be picked off individually.

Joshua's response, marching all night from Gilgal in the Jordan valley up into the hill country to reach Gibeon, covers a demanding climb of some twenty miles in darkness, arriving with enough surprise to catch the coalition unprepared, verse 9. The battle then runs along the descent from Beth-horon toward Azekah, a narrow, steep mountain pass that funnels a retreating army into an exposed column, exactly the kind of terrain where a violent hailstorm sweeping down the slope would do the damage the text describes, more killed by the hailstones than by the swords of the Israelites, verse 11.

Placing a conquered king's neck beneath the victor's foot, as the commanders do to the five captured kings in verse 24, is attested in the art and inscriptions of surrounding cultures as a recognized gesture of total, humiliating subjugation, not an improvised insult; Joshua turns the gesture immediately into a lesson for his own commanders rather than mere theater. The Book of Jashar, cited here and again at David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, 2 Samuel 1:18, was evidently a now-lost collection of Israelite victory and memorial poetry, suggesting that the sun-standing-still tradition was celebrated in song before it was ever set down in the prose history that survives.
context.canonical:
The chapter's central claim, that the LORD fights for His people while they stand nearly silent, is not new with Joshua; it restates almost word for word what Moses told a terrified Israel at the shore of the sea, the LORD will fight for you, you need only to be still, Exodus 14:14. Joshua 10 answers that earlier promise with a demonstration on dry land, hail and a halted sun replacing the parted water and drowned army, so that the same divine warrior who acted once at the beginning of Israel's story acts again near the story's fulfillment.

Other Scripture returns to this day as a fixed point of reference for God's power over creation itself. Habakkuk, centuries later, prays that God would repeat such deeds, sun and moon stood still in their places at the flash of Your flying arrows, Habakkuk 3:11, treating Joshua's day as the paradigm case of God bending the created order to save His people. The hailstorm finds its own echo in worship, He hurled lightning and routed them, hailstones and coals of fire, Psalm 18:12-14, language that reads almost as commentary on Beth-horon.

The New Testament takes up the chapter's climactic image, feet upon the necks of defeated kings, and drives it to its final horizon: Christ must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet, and the last enemy to be destroyed is death, 1 Corinthians 15:25-26, while Paul assures ordinary believers that the same crushing will be theirs in Him, the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet, Romans 16:20. A single day's victory over five Amorite kings becomes, across the canon, the template for the final defeat of every power that opposes God's people.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The writer wants no reader to conclude that Israel's growing string of victories reflects growing Israelite skill. Every device in the chapter works against that conclusion: the enemy is thrown into panic before Israel's swords do anything, more die by hail than by the army's own weapons, and the single most astonishing event of the whole conquest, the sun and moon standing still, happens not because Joshua commands brilliantly but because he prays boldly and the LORD listens to the voice of a man, verse 14. By narrating the battle almost as an afterthought to three successive divine interventions, the author is training Israel, and every later reader, to locate the source of victory outside the camp rather than inside it. He also wants the totality of the southern campaign, city after city, in one campaign, verse 42, understood as the direct fulfillment of centuries-old promise rather than a lucky run of successful sieges, so that the generation who first heard this account would trace their inherited land back not to their fathers' valor but to the LORD who fought for them before they were born.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter records a unique, unrepeated event, both the astronomical sign and the total destruction of the cities under the ban, and prescribes neither as a pattern for later warfare or later prayer. No church is authorized to expect the sun to stop for its own military or personal ambitions, and the herem carried out here belongs to a specific covenant command tied to Canaan's accumulated wickedness, not to any people or enterprise afterward, 2 Corinthians 10:3-4. What does transfer is the theology the narrative keeps insisting on: that the outcome of conflict, of any kind a believer faces, belongs finally to God rather than to human resource, and that bold, specific prayer, asking for what genuinely seems impossible, is not presumption when it is offered, as Joshua's was, in the presence of Israel and in the confidence of a word already spoken by the LORD, verse 8, rather than as an independent demand made apart from His will.

debates.question: How should the sun standing still be understood?

views.label: A literal, cosmic suspension of the sun and moon's motion
views.case: The text states plainly that the sun stopped in the middle of the sky and delayed going down about a full day, verse 13, and frames it as unrepeatable, there has been no day like it before or since, language that reads as historical claim rather than poetic flourish; the God who spoke the sun into existence, Genesis 1:16, can as easily halt its apparent motion for a day.

views.label: An extended or unusually bright day described in observational, poetic terms
views.case: The account is explicitly drawn from a poetic source, the Book of Jashar, and ancient observational language regularly describes the sun as moving across the sky from the vantage of the one who sees it rather than making claims about the earth's rotation; on this view God may have extended daylight, perhaps through unusual atmospheric refraction accompanying the hailstorm, without the text intending a technical statement about celestial mechanics.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm exactly what the narrator draws his own conclusion from, that the LORD listened to the voice of a man and fought for Israel, verse 14; the passage's theological weight rests on God's power and His attentiveness to prayer, not on settling a scientific question it was never written to answer.

debates.question: How can the total destruction commanded and carried out against these southern cities be reconciled with God's justice and mercy?

views.label: Long-delayed judgment on ripened, entrenched sin
views.case: God tells Abraham centuries earlier that the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete, Genesis 15:16, implying patient restraint rather than casual cruelty, and Deuteronomy insists Israel possesses the land because of these nations' wickedness, not Israel's own righteousness, Deuteronomy 9:4-5; the destruction here is carried out just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded, verse 40, framing it as obedient execution of a sentence long deserved rather than an act of national ambition.

views.label: A bounded, unrepeatable episode that foreshadows final judgment rather than modeling ongoing warfare
views.case: The herem is never extended past this conquest generation and this land, and mercy remains genuinely available within the very narrative that carries it out, as Rahab and Gibeon both show; the New Testament explicitly redirects the church's warfare away from the physical altogether, our weapons are not the weapons of the world, 2 Corinthians 10:4, treating the conquest as a signpost toward a final divine reckoning with evil rather than a precedent for any later people to imitate with the sword.

debates.bearing: Held together, both views insist that God's judgment in this chapter is neither impulsive nor a warrant for human violence in His name; it is bounded, commanded, and just, and it points forward to a final judgment where the same God who fought visibly for Israel at Beth-horon will finally set all things right.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the panic, the stillness, the ban, and the fighting already named, a handful of further details reward attention. Adoni-zedek's own name, built from adon, lord, and tsedeq, righteousness, echoes the earlier king of Jerusalem in Genesis 14:18, Melchizedek, king of righteousness, and may simply have functioned as a royal title carried by successive kings of that city rather than a personal name, which would mean Jerusalem's throne had claimed the language of righteousness for generations before David finally took the city that bore it.

The verb behind Joshua caught them by surprise in verse 9 is pathom, suddenly or unexpectedly, a rare adverbial form that stresses how completely the night march erased any chance of the coalition preparing a defense; the same abruptness marks God's own action two verses later, when He cast down, hishlik, hailstones from the sky, a verb of forceful throwing used elsewhere for hurling something down with deliberate, targeted force rather than mere falling weather.

Joshua's prayer in verse 12 addresses the sun directly with an imperative, dom, be still or be silent, the same root that gives damam its meaning elsewhere as ceasing or falling quiet, so that the sun is commanded almost as one commands a person to stop speaking or moving, an unusually intimate address to a created thing that many ancient peoples, including Canaan's own inhabitants, worshiped as a deity in its own right; Joshua's God, by contrast, simply speaks to it as one more part of His creation, obedient to His voice.

Verse 14 calls this a day like no other because the LORD shama, listened to, the voice of a man, the same verb used of hearing prayer elsewhere, but used here of something closer to obeying a request, underscoring that the miracle is not merely God acting but God responding to Joshua's specific, spoken word. And the verb of putting the kings' bodies away at sunset, verse 27, uses the same root, shaqa, to sink or set, that describes the sun itself going down, a small verbal echo linking the day's beginning, an unnaturally prolonged sun, to its ending, bodies finally allowed to sink out of sight as the natural day at last resumes and evening finally comes exactly where the narrative first held it back.

typology.type: The LORD fighting for Israel while the battle is still being decided
typology.fulfillment: Israel marches, but the deciding blows, panic, hail, a halted sun, are struck before or apart from any Israelite sword, so that human effort follows God's action rather than producing it. That pattern anticipates the whole logic of the cross, where the decisive victory over sin, death, and the powers is accomplished entirely by God in Christ, disarming the rulers and authorities and making a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross, Colossians 2:15, before any believer contributes anything at all. The type is incomplete because Joshua's victory still required a night march and a sword afterward; Christ's victory at the cross required nothing further from anyone to be finished, it is finished, John 19:30.

typology.type: The commanders' feet placed on the necks of the five defeated kings
typology.fulfillment: The gesture in verse 24 stages total, humiliating subjection in a single physical image, and Joshua immediately generalizes it, the LORD will do this to all the enemies you fight, verse 25, turning one battle's outcome into a standing promise. Paul takes the same image and stretches it across the whole of history, Christ must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet, 1 Corinthians 15:25, and to your feet, the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet, Romans 16:20. Where five kings under five commanders' feet pictured one victory, the final form places every hostile power, the last of them death itself, under Christ's feet permanently, 1 Corinthians 15:26.

typology.type: Hail from heaven doing more damage than Israel's own swords
typology.fulfillment: The text takes obvious care to note that more of them were killed by the hailstones than by the swords of the Israelites, verse 11, deliberately subordinating human weaponry to a weapon no army possesses. That subordination anticipates Paul's description of the church's own warfare, the weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world, instead they have divine power to demolish strongholds, 2 Corinthians 10:4, and the psalmist's confession that some trust in chariots and horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD, Psalm 20:7. The type is partial because the hail was still a physical weapon striking physical enemies; the greater warfare it foreshadows is fought and won in an entirely different register, against arguments and every presumption raised against the knowledge of God.

typology.type: A single, unrepeatable day given for the completion of God's people's victory
typology.fulfillment: There has been no day like it before or since, verse 14, marks this as a once-only intervention, time itself bent for the sake of a finished task. Scripture elsewhere anticipates another day set apart in the same way, a day of the LORD unlike any before it, and ultimately a day when time as currently ordered gives way entirely to the presence of God, Revelation 21:23, no need of sun or moon to shine, for the glory of God illuminates the city. Joshua's elongated day, sun and moon obedient to a man's prayer, is a small, early sign of a day coming when sun and moon will no longer be needed at all.

study.christ:
The refrain that structures this whole chapter, the LORD fought for Israel, is the theological seed of the entire gospel pattern: a people who cannot save themselves are saved by a God who fights on their behalf and asks only that they follow where He has already won. Israel's part in the victory, the night march, the pursuit, the final executions, comes after the panic, after the hail, after the sun stands still; the decisive action belongs entirely to the LORD. That order, God acts first and decisively, His people then act within a victory already secured, is exactly the order the gospel describes, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, Romans 5:8, the cross accomplished before any believer contributes faith, repentance, or obedience to the outcome it wins.

The image the chapter leaves stamped in the reader's mind, commanders' feet planted on the necks of five conquered kings, becomes one of the most sustained threads running from this book to the last one. Paul takes it up directly for the resurrection, for He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet, and the last enemy to be destroyed is death, 1 Corinthians 15:25-26, and again for the ordinary Christian life, the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet, Romans 16:20, so that what five commanders once did to five kings in a cave at Makkedah becomes the shape of what Christ will do to every power that has ever opposed Him, and what His people, united to Him, will share in doing as well.

And the sun that stands still at a man's prayer points toward a still greater reordering of creation around God's redemptive purposes. If the sun could be commanded to hold its course for the sake of a battle that secured an inheritance still only a shadow of what was to come, how much more will all things finally be brought into submission when the greater than Joshua returns, a day coming when there will be no more need of sun or moon, for the glory of God will illuminate the holy city and the Lamb will be its lamp, Revelation 21:23. The day at Gibeon was long; the day it points toward will simply never end.
study.god:
What this chapter shows about God begins with the strange intimacy of verse 12, Joshua speaks to the LORD in the presence of Israel, and asks for something no army had ever needed before, the sun to stop moving, and God does it. That a request this audacious could even be voiced, let alone granted, says something about the relationship this narrative assumes between God and the man leading His people: not a distant sovereign issuing orders from a safe remove but a God who listens to the voice of a man, verse 14, treating a battlefield prayer as worth answering with a suspension of the created order itself. Scripture rarely shows God's power and His nearness this plainly in the same sentence.

He is also, unmistakably, Lord over the very things the surrounding nations worshiped as gods. Canaanite religion gave the sun and moon divine status; this chapter has them obey a spoken command as unremarkably as a servant obeys a master, quietly stripping them of any claim to independent divinity without the narrator needing to argue the point directly. The same God who parted a sea for Moses' generation now halts the sky for Joshua's, showing that the created order itself, sun, moon, weather, has no autonomy from Him at any point in Israel's history.

His justice and His faithfulness meet in the hailstones as much as in the halted sun. The stones fall specifically on a coalition that gathered to punish a city for making peace, so that judgment lands on aggression against those under God's protection, while faithfulness to His earlier promise, to give the whole land to Israel, drives the entire campaign forward one city at a time. And His refusal to let the victory be credited to anything but Himself, panic before contact, hail before swords, silence before Joshua ever draws his own blade, is not incidental narrative color; it is the chapter's whole argument, repeated in its opening declaration and its closing summary alike, that this God alone is the one who fights, and therefore He alone deserves the glory for what fighting accomplishes.

crossReferences.note: Moses tells a terrified Israel at the sea, the LORD will fight for you, you need only to be still. The same divine warrior who parted the water for the first generation halts the sky for the second, the identical promise proven true across a whole generation's distance.

God is pictured hurling hailstones and lightning to rout His enemies, imagery that reads almost as a hymn written to commemorate the very storm that struck the coalition fleeing down the descent from Beth-horon.

Sun and moon stood still in their places at the flash of Your flying arrows, a later prophet praying for God to repeat the exact wonder of Joshua's day as proof that the same warrior who saved Israel once can save again.

The LORD is said to rise up as in the Valley of Gibeon to do His strange work, naming this very battlefield centuries later as the paradigm case of God acting decisively and unexpectedly on His people's behalf, even when His action is judgment rather than rescue.

Christ must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet, and the last enemy to be destroyed is death. The image of feet placed on the necks of Joshua's five captured kings becomes, in Paul's hands, the shape of the final resurrection victory.

Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross. Like the battle at Gibeon, the decisive victory is accomplished by God directly, before any human party contributes to the outcome.

The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet, extending the very image of subjugated kings from Joshua 10 to ordinary believers, who are promised to share personally in the crushing of their ultimate enemy.

The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world but carry divine power to demolish strongholds. Joshua's hailstones outperforming Israelite swords already illustrates that the decisive weapon in God's battles is never the merely human one.
Some trust in chariots and horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God, the very confession Joshua 10 dramatizes by having Israel win a battle its own swords barely finish.

study.oneStory:
By the time the five Amorite kings gather at Gibeon, Israel has already seen the LORD deliver Jericho by a shout and Ai by an ambush, but chapter 10 pushes the pattern further than either, into the realm of the largest army yet faced and the most extraordinary sign yet given. The chapter answers a question the whole conquest keeps raising in different forms, will the LORD who promised this land to Abraham actually secure it, and its answer is emphatic rather than gradual: not only does He secure it, He does so in a way that leaves no room for Israel to imagine the outcome depended on numbers, weapons, or strategy. Panic, hail, a halted sun, three separate wonders stacked inside a single day, close off every alternative explanation before the narrator even lists which cities fell next.

That emphatic answer feeds directly into everything that follows in Israel's story. The refrain the LORD fought for Israel becomes the theological backbone the rest of the conquest narrative leans on through chapter 11's northern campaign and into the settled life the book of Judges will eventually forget, to Israel's repeated cost. When later generations trust chariots and alliances instead of the God who once stopped the sky for their fathers, the warning implicit in this chapter's insistence on divine rather than human causation becomes the very failure the prophets keep diagnosing.

The chapter's furthest reach, though, runs forward rather than backward. The image of conquered kings beneath victors' feet becomes, across the whole canon, the shape of the final defeat of every power opposed to God, sin, death, and the devil himself, subdued not by any army but by the obedience and resurrection of Christ, who fights the battle His people could never fight and wins it before they are even asked to lift a sword. What began as an untimely-long day over a mountain pass in Canaan becomes, by the last page of Scripture, the promise of an unending day in a city that needs no sun at all, because the glory of God and of the Lamb is its light.

quiz.q: Why did the five Amorite kings attack Gibeon?

options.text: Because Gibeon, a great city, had made peace with Israel and defected from the Canaanite side.
options.note: Verses 1 to 5 show the kings alarmed that mighty Gibeon had allied with Israel.

options.text: Because Gibeon had attacked them first.
options.note: Gibeon had not attacked them; the kings moved against it for making peace with Israel.

options.text: Because Gibeon controlled the only water in the region.
options.note: The reason given is Gibeon's peace with Israel, not control of water.

options.text: Because Joshua ordered them to attack Gibeon.
options.note: Joshua defended Gibeon; the enemy kings, not Joshua, launched the attack.

quiz.q: How did God fight for Israel in this battle?

options.text: He threw the enemy into panic, killed many with hailstones, and made the sun stand still.
options.note: Verses 10 to 14 credit the panic, the hail, and the halted sun all to the LORD.

options.text: He sent an angel to fight the kings in single combat.
options.note: God intervened powerfully, but through panic, hail, and the halted sun, not an angel in single combat.

options.text: He gave Israel superior weapons and armor.
options.note: The victory came from God's direct acts, not better equipment.

options.text: He did nothing; Israel won purely by its night march.
options.note: The night march gained surprise, but the text says the LORD fought for Israel with panic, hail, and the sun.

quiz.q: What was extraordinary about the day of this battle?

options.text: At Joshua's prayer the sun stood still, and there was no day like it, for the LORD listened to a man.
options.note: Verses 12 to 14 record the unique day when the sun stood still at Joshua's request.

options.text: It was the shortest day in Israel's history.
options.note: The reverse: the day was lengthened, not shortened, so Israel could complete the victory.

options.text: A total eclipse hid the battle from the enemy.
options.note: There was no eclipse; the sun stood still and prolonged the daylight.

options.text: Nothing unusual happened that day.
options.note: The narrator says there had been no day like it before or since; it was utterly unique.

quiz.q: What did placing feet on the necks of the kings signify?

options.text: Complete victory over the enemy, and assurance that the LORD would do the same to all Israel's foes.
options.note: Verses 24 to 25 make it a sign of total conquest and a spur to courage.

options.text: A ritual of mercy sparing the kings' lives.
options.note: It was not mercy; the kings were then executed. It signified total defeat, not sparing them.

options.text: A way of honoring the defeated kings.
options.note: It dishonored and subdued them; it was a sign of conquest, not honor.

options.text: A superstitious rite with no meaning.
options.note: It was a recognized sign of total victory and an encouragement to trust God for future battles.

quiz.q: How much of the southern region fell, and to whom is the victory credited?

options.text: The whole southern region fell in one campaign, because the LORD fought for Israel.
options.note: Verses 40 to 42 credit the sweeping, single-campaign victory to the LORD fighting for Israel.

options.text: Only Gibeon was saved, and no other cities were taken.
options.note: Far more than Gibeon; the whole south fell, and the credit goes to the LORD.

options.text: The cities fell over many years of gradual warfare.
options.note: The text stresses one campaign, not many years, precisely because God fought for them.

options.text: Israel conquered it all by its own superior strategy.
options.note: The victory is explicitly credited to the LORD who fought for Israel, not to human strategy.

questions: The refrain of the chapter is that the LORD fought for Israel. Where in your life are you trying to fight a battle in your own strength that you need to entrust to the God who fights for His people?
Joshua prayed a bold, almost unthinkable prayer, and God answered. What would it look like for you to bring bolder prayers to the God who commands even the sun and moon?
God defended the Gibeonites because Israel had sworn to protect them, even though the alliance began in failure. How does God's faithfulness to His word encourage you when you have made mistakes?

The commanders put their feet on the necks of the kings as a sign of victory, pointing to Christ under whose feet every enemy will be placed. How does knowing Christ's final victory over sin and death shape your courage today?
The whole south fell in one campaign, and the glory went to God alone. Where are you tempted to take credit for what is really God's doing, and how can you give Him the glory instead?

translationNotes.note: Devoted it to destruction renders a form of the Hebrew cherem, recurring in verses 28, 35, 37, 39, and 40.

Verses 12 and 13 quote a poetic fragment; the poem lines have been joined in order as running text. The BSB footnote points to the Book of Jashar, an old collection of Israelite poetry now lost, also cited in 2 Samuel 1:18.
Hung their bodies on five trees renders a phrase the BSB footnote also gives as impaled on five poles; the bodies were taken down by evening, as in verse 27 and per Deuteronomy 21:22-23.
